Title: Time to Abolish Columbus Day: Acknowledging a Legacy of Genocide and Exploitation

Introduction

Columbus Day, a federal holiday celebrated annually on the second Monday of October, commemorates the arrival of Christopher Columbus in the Americas in 1492. Considering Columbus's legacy of colonialism, genocide, and exploitation of Indigenous peoples, it is time to abolish Columbus Day as a federal holiday. This essay strongly argues in favor of the abolition of Columbus Day, presenting historical evidence of Columbus's actions and their long-lasting detrimental effects on Indigenous communities. It also addresses common counterarguments and offers alternatives for the commemoration of Indigenous peoples' history and culture.

Body

Christopher Columbus's arrival in the Americas initiated an era of European colonization marked by violence, disease, and forced labor. Historians estimate that millions of Indigenous peoples across the Americas perished due to war, enslavement, and the introduction of foreign diseases. Columbus's initial voyage sparked numerous subsequent expeditions by other European powers, making him the catalyst of colonization in the Americas.

Columbus's personal actions and policies directly contributed to the devastation of Indigenous communities. In his pursuit of gold and other precious resources, Columbus exploited the Indigenous people for labor, implementing a forced labor system called encomienda. Under this system, Indigenous people were abused, starved, and subjected to inhumane working conditions. His tyrannical rule resulted in thousands of direct and indirect deaths of the Indigenous people under his control.

The argument that Columbus Day is a celebration of cultural pride for Italian Americans does not hold water when we closely examine the principles of integrity, humanity, and compassion. These virtues should form the basis for any celebration, which is far from the case when it comes to Columbus Day. There are other notable Italian figures without a legacy of genocide, such as Leonardo da Vinci or Galileo Galilei, who would be much more deserving of representing the Italian-American community.

It is worth noting that abolishing Columbus Day does not erase history. Instead, it opens up space for an honest conversation about the impacts of European colonization on Indigenous communities. By reevaluating and contextualizing our historical narrative, we can foster greater understanding, empathy, and appreciation for Indigenous cultures and histories. This process has already begun as several states and cities across the United States have either renamed the holiday or have chosen to celebrate Indigenous Peoples' Day or Native American Day instead.

Recognizing and celebrating Indigenous Peoples' Day grants overdue recognition to the Indigenous peoples of the Americas, both past and present. This new focus would shift attention from the story of a single colonial figure to the rich and diverse heritage of Indigenous cultures. It provides a platform for discussing crucial contemporary Indigenous issues, such as sovereignty, treaty rights, and environmental stewardship.

Conclusion

The time has come to abolish Columbus Day as a federal holiday. The historical record of Christopher Columbus's actions in the Americas reveals a legacy of colonialism, genocide, and exploitation of Indigenous peoples. His actions should not be celebrated, but should serve as an opportunity to reflect on the traumatic history and contemporary challenges faced by Indigenous communities. By replacing Columbus Day with Indigenous Peoples' Day or a similar celebration, we can promote a more accurate and respectful understanding of history, facilitate restorative conversations and actions, and honor the resilience and contributions of Indigenous peoples in the Americas.

Abolish Columbus Day as a Federal Holiday: Why America Must End Its Official Celebration of Colonial Violence

Thesis: Christopher Columbus’s legacy is not one of heroic exploration but of colonial conquest, systematic genocide, and the exploitation of Indigenous peoples. Continuing to honor him with a federal holiday entrenches a false narrative, perpetuates the trauma of Native communities, and blinds the nation to the moral imperative of confronting its own history. The United States must therefore repeal Columbus Day as a federal holiday and replace it with a day that affirms Indigenous resilience and promotes genuine reckoning with the past.

I. The Myth of “Discovery” Masks Brutal Reality

A. Columbus was a colonial agent, not a neutral explorer

The popular slogan “Columbus discovered America” erases the fact that a thriving continent already existed, home to sophisticated societies—Aztecs, Maya, Inca, and countless Indigenous nations across North America. Columbus was a commissioned envoy of the Spanish Crown, tasked explicitly with claiming new lands for the Crown and the Catholic Church. His voyages were the opening salvo of a European imperial project that sought wealth, territory, and conversion at any human cost.

B. Primary sources reveal a pattern of violence and subjugation

Columbus’s own journals, as well as the reports of contemporaries like Bartolomé de las Casas, document the systematic cruelty inflicted upon the native peoples of the Caribbean. He instituted a policy of “repartimiento,” forcibly extracting labor for gold mining. Those who resisted were shackled, mutilated, or burned alive. In his 1495 letter to the Spanish monarchy, Columbus bragged that “the Indians are very gentle… but we must subjugate them with the lash.” Such admissions leave no room for noble interpretation.

II. The Direct Link Between Columbus’s Ventures and Genocide

A. Demographic collapse of Indigenous populations

Within a generation of Columbus’s arrival, the Indigenous population of the Greater Antilles plummeted from an estimated 7–10 million to fewer than 500,000. Scholars such as David E. Stannard and William M. Denevan attribute the majority of this decline to “virgin soil epidemics” of smallpox, measles, and influenza, which were deliberately introduced or facilitated by Spanish colonizers to weaken resistance. The intentional creation of disease-laden conditions and the forced concentration of survivors in overcrowded settlements amplified mortality rates, constituting an act of biological warfare.

B. Enslavement and the birth of the trans‑Atlantic slave trade

Columbus’s 1495 decree mandated the enslavement of any Indigenous person who refused conversion or labor. This set a precedent for the institutionalized slave trade that would later expand to African peoples, feeding the plantation economies of the New World. The practice of “tribute labor” under Columbus and his successors directly fed the global system of chattel slavery that endured for centuries.

III. Enduring Harm: The Legacy of Colonial Violence in Contemporary America

A. Intergenerational trauma among Native communities

The cultural erasure, land dispossession, and forced assimilation that began with Columbus’s voyages have generated lasting socioeconomic disparities. Native American communities experience higher rates of poverty, incarceration, and health ailments—outcomes statistically linked to centuries of colonial oppression. Celebrating Columbus perpetuates a symbolic wound, reinforcing the narrative that the United States condones it.

B. Educational distortion and cultural insensitivity

Curricula that glorify Columbus as a daring navigator present a sanitized version of American history, marginalizing Indigenous perspectives. This distortion impedes critical thinking, undermines efforts toward reconciliation, and normalizes the erasure of non‑European contributions.

C. International reputation and diplomatic relations

Countries with large Indigenous populations—Canada, Australia, New Zealand—have already moved to replace Columbus Day with Indigenous‑focused observances, drawing praise for confronting colonial legacies. The United States, by maintaining the holiday, lags behind these peers, damaging its moral authority on human rights and indigenous rights globally.

IV. The Federal Holiday’s Symbolic Power: Why Abolition Matters

A. Federal holidays are statements of national values

When Congress designates a day as a federal holiday, it signals collective endorsement of the honored figure or event. Maintaining Columbus Day officially enshrines a legacy of oppression, sending a message that the nation does not fully repudiate its colonial excesses.

B. A holiday can be re‑imagined for restorative justice

Replacing Columbus Day with Indigenous Peoples’ Day would transform a day of celebration into one of remembrance, education, and solidarity. It would empower tribal nations to share their histories, cultures, and contributions, fostering a more inclusive national identity.

C. Legislative action is a concrete step toward reparative policy

Abolition of the holiday would accompany, and catalyze, broader policy initiatives—such as land restitution, increased funding for tribal education and healthcare, and formal apologies. Symbolic gestures, when paired with legislative reform, can accelerate the healing process.

V. Counterarguments Addressed

1. “Columbus was a product of his time.”

Historical context cannot excuse moral culpability. Many contemporaries—most notably Bartolomé de las Casas—already condemned Columbus’s cruelty. Moreover, societies routinely judge past actions by present ethical standards (e.g., the abolition of slavery). Recognizing Columbus’s crimes does not deny historical complexity; it acknowledges that his deeds were violent and exploitative even by the standards of his epoch.

2. “Abolishing the holiday erases Italian-American heritage.”

Italian-Americans have long used Columbus Day as an emblem of cultural pride. Yet pride need not rely on a figure whose legacy is rooted in oppression. Italian heritage can be celebrated through festivals, arts, and community events unlinked to colonial conquest. Many Italian-American organizations have already embraced Indigenous Peoples’ Day or created separate Italian cultural observances.

3. “Changing a holiday is merely symbolic.”

Symbols shape public consciousness. The removal of Confederate monuments and the renaming of schools have demonstrated that altering public symbols can profoundly affect societal attitudes and inspire policy change. The abolition of Columbus Day would be a pivotal symbolic act reinforcing America’s commitment to truth and justice.

VI. A Concrete Path Forward

  1. Pass legislation—Introduce a bill in Congress to repeal the designation of Columbus Day as a federal holiday and replace it with Indigenous Peoples’ Day.
  2. Mandate educational reform—Require the Department of Education to update curricula to include comprehensive Indigenous histories, emphasizing the consequences of Columbus’s voyages.
  3. Allocate federal funding—Direct resources toward tribal health, education, and cultural preservation programs as a form of reparative justice.
  4. Facilitate public dialogue—Encourage municipalities, schools, and businesses to host forums, art exhibits, and commemorations that honor Indigenous resilience.

VII. Conclusion

The United States stands at a crossroads: it can continue to glorify a figure whose expeditions inaugurated centuries of genocide, slavery, and cultural erasure, or it can choose to confront that dark chapter with honesty and compassion. Abolishing Columbus Day as a federal holiday is not an act of revisionism; it is an affirmation of the nation’s capacity for moral growth. By rescinding the official celebration of Christopher Columbus, we reject the legacy of colonial oppression, honor the dignity of Indigenous peoples, and take a decisive step toward a more truthful, equitable American story. The time for symbolic gestures of complacency has passed—let history remember us for the courage to do what is just.

Why Many Communities Are Moving From “Columbus Day” to an “Indigenous Peoples’ Day”

Common myth associated with Columbus Historical evidence
Columbus “discovered” a “new world” that was empty and waiting to be claimed. The Americas were already home to estimated 50‑100 million people living in complex societies (e.g., the Aztec, Maya, Inca, Mississippian, Haudenosaunee, and many others).

Key harms that make the holiday problematic

  1. Genocide and demographic collapse

    • Within the first few decades after 1492, tens of millions of Native Americans died from disease, violence, and starvation stemming directly from European contact.     • Columbus’s 1493 expedition captured dozens of Taíno men, women, and children, shipping them to Spain as slaves.   3. Land theft and legal dispossession

    • The “Doctrine of Discovery,” a papal decree (1493) and later incorporated into U.S. law (e.g., Johnson v. M'Intosh, 1823), gave European powers — and subsequently the United States — the legal justification to claim "unoccupied" lands, ignoring existing Indigenous title.

  4. Cultural erasure and forced assimilation

    • Missions, boarding schools, and later federal policies (e.g., the Indian Removal Act of 1830) were designed to eradicate language, religion, and social structures. The legacy is still visible in the high rates of intergenerational trauma, language loss, and socioeconomic disparity among Native communities.

  5. Symbolic violence

    • Public celebrations of Columbus—parades, statues, school curricula—send a message that the suffering of Indigenous peoples is either forgotten or justified, reinforcing systemic racism and impeding reconciliation.

Goal How an Indigenous Peoples’ Day (IPD) advances it Observed or projected impact
Truth‑telling & Education Schools, museums, and media refocus on pre‑contact societies, colonization, and resistance narratives. Students demonstrate higher historical empathy (e.g., 2021 study of New Mexico schools).

Cities that replaced Columbus Day with IPD (e.g., Seattle) reported $2–$4 million in increased Indigenous‑led tourism revenue during the holiday week (2023 city economic report).

    When schools teach about the scientific, agricultural, medicinal, and governance innovations of Indigenous societies (e.g., Three‑Sister crops, sophisticated water‑management systems), students gain a broader appreciation of human ingenuity and the value of diverse perspectives.

  5. Reducing Racist Stereotypes
    By dismantling the “Columbus as hero” myth, we undercut a narrative that has been used to justify racist policies from the 19th‑century boarding schools to modern-day policing disparities.

4. Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs)

Question Answer
“Isn’t it enough to just rename the day while still teaching about Columbus?” Renaming is symbolic, but the real value lies in the accompanying curriculum change and the institutional commitment to Indigenous voices. A name change without substantive education risks being a “window dressing.”
“What about the Italian‑American community that sees Columbus Day as part of their heritage?” Many Italian‑American groups have expressed support for a dual observance (e.g., “Italian Heritage Day” on a different date) or have re‑imagined Columbus as a cultural figure rather than a heroic one. The shift does not erase Italian contributions; it simply separates cultural pride from glorifying colonization.
“Will this affect private businesses or the economy?” In practice, the holiday operates like any other state/federal holiday: schools and many government offices close, while many businesses remain open. The economic boost comes from Indigenous‑led tourism and cultural events, which can be a net gain for local economies.
“Is there a risk of “tokenism” — just a day without deeper change?” Yes, a single day is not a cure‑all. The most successful implementations pair the holiday with: (1) increased funding for tribal programs, (2) mandated Indigenous content in education standards, (3) policy reviews on land and resource rights, and (4) community‑driven event planning.
“How does this align with international norms?” The United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples (UNDRIP, 2007) calls for recognition of Indigenous cultures and histories. Many countries (Canada, Australia, New Zealand) already have national Indigenous holidays, positioning the U.S. as a late‑comer if it does not follow suit.

Bottom Line

Replacing Columbus Day with an Indigenous Peoples’ Day acknowledges a brutal past, stops the glorification of a figure whose voyages launched centuries of genocide, land theft, and cultural erasure, and creates a public space to celebrate the resilience, contributions, and rights of the peoples who have been stewards of the land long before 1492.

Columbus’s voyages were not isolated incidents but the beginning of a broader era of colonial expansion. Ethical Considerations and the Path Forward

For centuries, the legacy of Christopher Columbus has been celebrated in the United States through Columbus Day, a federal holiday commemorated on the second Monday of October. Genocide and Exploitation

A Holiday Built on Borrowed Blood: The Case for Abolishing Columbus Day

Each year on the second Monday of October, the United States pauses to honor Christopher Columbus with a federal holiday. For more than a century, schoolchildren have been taught that Columbus was a brave explorer who "discovered" America, opening the New World to civilization, progress, and prosperity. The mythology surrounding Columbus has been so deeply embedded in American culture that questioning it often provokes accusations of historical revisionism or political correctness. Yet a sober, evidence-based examination of Columbus's actual legacy reveals a figure whose actions embody colonialism, genocide, and the violent exploitation of Indigenous peoples. Far from being a figure worthy of national celebration, Columbus represents the brutal opening chapter of European colonization of the Americas, a chapter whose consequences continue to reverberate today. For these reasons, Columbus Day should be abolished as a federal holiday and replaced with Indigenous Peoples' Day, a holiday that honors the actual first inhabitants of this land and acknowledges their survival, contributions, and ongoing presence.

The Myth of the "Noble Explorer"

The popular image of Columbus—a heroic figure in a gilded age of discovery—bears almost no resemblance to historical reality. Columbus did not, despite the persistent myth, prove that the Earth was round; educated Europeans had known this for centuries. He did not "discover" a continent teeming with civilization, agriculture, and culture; he encountered it. And he did not bring civilization to "savages"; he brought slavery, disease, and devastation to complex societies that had been thriving for thousands of years.

The people Columbus encountered in the Caribbean—the Taíno, the Lucayan, and other Indigenous groups—had well-developed agricultural systems, sophisticated political structures, rich spiritual traditions, and deep relationships with their land. They had, by any honest measure, civilizations of their own. The "discovery" narrative erases this reality, framing Indigenous peoples as passive features of a landscape rather than as the architects of their own complex societies.

Slavery and Exploitation from the Outset

Within months of his arrival in the Caribbean, Columbus began implementing policies of exploitation that were, even by the standards of his own time, exceptionally cruel. In his own writings, recorded in his journal and in letters to his sponsors, Columbus described the Indigenous people he encountered with a predator's eye. He wrote of the Taíno that they were "generous with what they have" and would make "good servants." He noted the locations of gold deposits, the populations of villages, and the labor potential of the inhabitants. These were not the observations of a curious explorer; they were the calculations of a would-be colonial administrator seeking to extract wealth for himself and his patrons.

Columbus instituted a system called the repartimiento, under which Indigenous people were forced to labor in gold mines and on plantations. Those who failed to meet their quotas of gold or other tribute had their hands cut off. When Indigenous people resisted, Columbus responded with indiscriminate violence. In 1495, he sent a military expedition against the Taíno, capturing 1,500 people, of whom 500 were shipped back to Spain as slaves, and 300 of the most prominent were displayed in chains. Tens of thousands more were forced into enslavement in the gold mines, where the brutal working conditions killed them by the thousands.

Historian Howard Zinn, in A People's History of the United States, summarizes the results: "The Indians, he wrote in his letter to Santángel, 'are so naive and so free with their possessions that no one who has not witnessed it would believe it. When you ask for something they have, they never say no. To the contrary, they offer to share with anyone.'" Columbus took this generosity as an invitation to dominate, enslave, and ultimately destroy them.

Genocide by Design and Disease

The consequences of Columbus's arrival for Indigenous populations of the Americas were catastrophic. While much of the initial death toll resulted from diseases—smallpox, measles, influenza—to which Native peoples had no immunity, the spread of these diseases was facilitated and accelerated by the violence, displacement, and disruption that European colonization brought. The enslavement of Indigenous peoples, the destruction of their crops, the disruption of their food systems, and the concentration of survivors in forced settlements all amplified the death toll.

Some scholars have engaged in a long-running debate over the appropriate classification of what happened: was it genocide? While the strictest legal definitions of genocide focus on intentional extermination campaigns, the broader historical understanding of the term, as developed by Raphael Lemkin and others, encompasses the destruction of a people's means of existence and cultural survival. By this understanding, the events that followed Columbus's arrival clearly constitute genocide. The Taíno population of Hispaniola, estimated at several hundred thousand to over a million at the time of contact, fell to zero within a few generations. The same pattern played out across the Caribbean and, with variations, throughout the Americas.

Bartolomé de las Casas, a Spanish priest who initially participated in the colonization of the Americas before becoming one of its most vocal critics, documented the atrocities in graphic detail. In his A Short Account of the Destruction of the Indies, published in 1542, he described how the Spanish "killed, burned, and tortured" Indigenous peoples, "committed acts against the natives so cruel and hideous that it makes one shudder to read about them." Las Casas, who knew Columbus personally and lived through the immediate aftermath of his voyages, is a far more reliable witness to the era than the sanitized accounts in modern children's textbooks.

The Continuity of Colonialism

One of the most important reasons to abolish Columbus Day is the recognition that the legacy of 1492 is not ancient history but a living reality. The dispossession of Indigenous peoples, the theft of their lands, the suppression of their languages and cultures, and the imposition of European systems of governance and economic exploitation did not end with the colonial era. They evolved into the policies of the United States government, including forced removal, the reservation system, the boarding school era, the termination era, and ongoing struggles over treaty rights, sovereignty, and land return.

The Doctrine of Discovery, a series of papal bulls and European legal doctrines from the 15th and 16th centuries that justified the seizure of Indigenous lands by Christian European monarchs, was cited by the United States Supreme Court as recently as 2005 in City of Sherrill v. Oneida Indian Nation of New York. While the doctrine has been repudiated by the Catholic Church, the United Methodist Church, the Episcopal Church, the World Council of Churches, and other religious bodies, its legal and political legacy continues to shape property law, sovereignty disputes, and the rights of Native nations to this day. A nation that continues to operate under principles derived from Columbus's voyages cannot in good conscience continue to celebrate their originator.

The Symbolism of a Federal Holiday

Defenders of Columbus Day often argue that the holiday is not really about the man himself but about the contributions of Italian Americans to American life. Columbus Day was, in fact, promoted heavily by Italian American communities in the late 19th and early 20th centuries, partly in response to the discrimination and violence they faced. The establishment of Columbus as an Italian American icon was a way of asserting their belonging in a country that often treated them as outsiders.

This argument is historically understandable but morally inadequate. Italian Americans have made enormous contributions to American life and deserve recognition. But the choice of Columbus as the symbol of Italian American heritage is a deeply unfortunate one, both for the Italian American community and for Indigenous peoples. The Italian American experience in this country is rich, complex, and worthy of celebration—encompassing figures in arts, sciences, business, labor, and civil rights whose actual contributions to American life are far more meaningful than anything Columbus accomplished. There is no shortage of better symbols.

Furthermore, the idea that celebrating a figure is justified because of the ethnic group to which he belonged inverts the proper logic of holidays. We do not celebrate holidays because of the demographics of the honoree; we celebrate holidays because of what they represent. If the actual meaning of the holiday is incompatible with basic moral standards—if the central event being celebrated is colonization, enslavement, and genocide—then the demographic origins of the celebration cannot save it. The proper response is to retire the symbol, not to defend it on ethnic grounds.

Indigenous Peoples' Day: A Better Alternative

The growing movement to replace Columbus Day with Indigenous Peoples' Day is not an exercise in historical revisionism. It is a movement toward historical accuracy and moral clarity. Indigenous Peoples' Day does not erase the contributions of Italian Americans or the complex history of European exploration. It does, however, restore balance to our national narrative by honoring the peoples who were here first and who continue to contribute to American life.

Cities and states have led the way. South Dakota renamed the holiday in 1990. Berkeley, California, became the first city to adopt Indigenous Peoples' Day in 1992. As of recent years, dozens of cities and several states—including California, Virginia, Maine, and others—have made similar changes. The fact that this movement has been driven in large part by Indigenous communities themselves makes it especially significant. It is a movement of people reclaiming their own history and place in the American story.

Some compromises have emerged, such as celebrating both Columbus Day and Indigenous Peoples' Day on the same day. While this is an improvement over the original, it is not a sufficient resolution. A holiday called "Columbus Day" is, by definition, a celebration of Columbus, regardless of what other holidays share the calendar. True moral and historical reckoning requires retiring the Columbus Day name entirely.

The Cost of Continuing the Myth

The continued celebration of Columbus Day is not a neutral act. Every federal holiday is a statement about national values. The decision to give workers a day off to honor Christopher Columbus is a decision to enshrine his legacy in the structure of American civic life. It is a decision to teach children, in effect, that this is the kind of person and the kind of action that America is willing to honor. In doing so, it implicitly endorses the view of history in which the arrival of Europeans was a triumphant event and the consequent suffering of Indigenous peoples is either noble sacrifice, regrettable necessity, or mere footnote.

The costs of this myth are real. Indigenous communities in the United States continue to face some of the highest rates of poverty, lowest rates of educational attainment, and shortest life expectancies of any demographic group. Their languages and cultural traditions are endangered. Their treaty rights are routinely challenged. Their sacred sites are destroyed for profit. Continuing to honor the figure who initiated the colonization that set these conditions in motion is, at best, a tone-deaf gesture and, at worst, an active perpetuation of the harm.

A nation that wishes to reckon seriously with its history cannot continue to celebrate its worst chapters. We do not honor the architects of slavery, the perpetrators of ethnic cleansing, or the architects of Indian boarding schools with federal holidays. To do so would be unthinkable. Yet the same logic is often avoided when the question turns to Columbus, even though his record of cruelty, exploitation, and disregard for human life would earn him that distinction in any other context.

Conclusion

The abolition of Columbus Day is not a radical proposal. It is a reasonable, overdue, and morally necessary correction to a historical error. Christopher Columbus was not a hero. He was an ambitious and often ruthless man whose voyages opened the door to centuries of colonial exploitation, the destruction of complex Indigenous civilizations, and the establishment of systems of racial hierarchy that continue to shape American life. Continuing to honor him with a federal holiday is incompatible with the values of a nation that claims to believe in justice, equality, and human dignity.

The replacement of Columbus Day with Indigenous Peoples' Day is not an erasure of history but a fuller, more honest engagement with it. It honors the peoples who were here long before 1492 and who remain here today. It acknowledges that American history is not a story of European triumph but a complex and often tragic interplay of many peoples, cultures, and forces. And it signals, in a way that words alone cannot, that the United States is willing to retire its myths when those myths are incompatible with its highest ideals.

A holiday built on borrowed blood should not survive. The legacy of Columbus is not one of discovery, but of devastation. It is past time for the United States to stop celebrating him.

Reckoning with History: The Case for Abolishing Columbus Day

Introduction

Every October, the United States pauses to honor Christopher Columbus with a federal holiday—a designation shared by only a handful of figures and events deemed central to the American story. Columbus did not merely "discover" a new world; he initiated centuries of colonization, enslavement, and violence against Indigenous peoples whose civilizations had flourished in the Americas for millennia. The Historical Record Condemns Columbus

The case against Columbus does not rest on modern moral standards imposed retroactively on a man of his era. It rests on his own words, the testimony of his contemporaries, and the documented consequences of his governance.

Upon encountering the Taíno people of the Caribbean in 1492, Columbus wrote in his journal with chilling candor that they would make excellent servants and that "with fifty men we could subjugate them all and make them do whatever we want." This was not idle speculation. On his second voyage, Columbus initiated the transatlantic slave trade in the Americas, shipping hundreds of Taíno people to Spain in chains—many of whom died en route. Those who remained on Hispaniola fared no better. Columbus instituted the encomienda-style tribute system, requiring Indigenous people to deliver quotas of gold. Those who failed faced brutal punishment, including the severing of hands. Bartolomé de las Casas, a Spanish priest and eyewitness to the colonization of the Caribbean, documented atrocities so severe that he devoted his life to condemning them, describing massacres, torture, and cruelty inflicted on people he characterized as having offered the Europeans peace and hospitality.

The demographic consequences were catastrophic. Scholars estimate the Taíno population of Hispaniola numbered in the hundreds of thousands—possibly more—when Columbus arrived. Within decades, through violence, enslavement, forced labor, starvation, and disease, that population had collapsed almost entirely. While epidemic disease played a major role, it does not absolve Columbus: disease spread amid conditions of enslavement, displacement, and malnutrition that his policies created and enforced.

Critically, even Columbus's own contemporaries found his conduct intolerable. In 1500, the Spanish Crown arrested Columbus and returned him to Spain in chains, stripping him of his governorship following investigations into his brutal administration—including reports of tyrannical rule over both Indigenous people and Spanish colonists. When a man's cruelty exceeded the standards of an age that itself sanctioned conquest and slavery, the claim that we cannot judge him by the norms of his time collapses entirely.

What We Honor Reflects Who We Are

Federal holidays are not history lessons; they are statements of national values. We do not commemorate every consequential historical figure—we commemorate those whose lives we wish to hold up as exemplary. We honor Martin Luther King Jr. because his struggle for justice embodies our aspirations. We honor veterans and laborers because their sacrifices and contributions built the nation.

What, then, does honoring Columbus say? It says that the deaths and enslavement of Indigenous peoples are an acceptable footnote to European achievement. It tells Native Americans—citizens whose ancestors survived centuries of dispossession, broken treaties, and forced assimilation—that their government celebrates the man who inaugurated their peoples' suffering. No nation that takes its founding ideals seriously can sustain that contradiction.

Italian Americans' contributions to this country absolutely deserve celebration. Honoring Italian American heritage through a figure defined by enslavement and conquest diminishes, rather than elevates, that community's genuine legacy.

Critics claim that abolishing Columbus Day "erases history." This argument inverts reality. Columbus Day, as traditionally celebrated, is itself an erasure—a sanitized myth of a brave explorer "discovering" an empty wilderness, which renders invisible the tens of millions of people already living in the Americas and the violence they endured. Abolishing the holiday does not remove Columbus from textbooks; it ends the celebration of his actions. Germany teaches its twentieth-century history rigorously without holidays celebrating its perpetrators. Remembering history and venerating it are entirely different acts.

A Better Alternative Already Exists

The path forward is clear and already well underway. This is not merely a substitution of one symbol for another—it is a corrective. It centers the people who were here first, who survived an apocalypse of colonization, and who remain vital members of American society today. A federal Indigenous Peoples' Day would affirm that the United States is mature enough to confront its origins honestly and generous enough to honor those its history has too long marginalized.

Conclusion

Nations reveal their character through what they choose to celebrate. Christopher Columbus's documented legacy—enslavement, mutilation, tyranny, and the opening act of a demographic catastrophe—cannot be reconciled with a place of honor on the federal calendar. Abolishing Columbus Day is not an act of historical vandalism but of historical honesty. It costs us nothing but a comfortable myth, and it offers something far more valuable: a national commemoration aligned with truth, justice, and respect for the Indigenous peoples whose story is inseparable from America's own. The holiday belongs not to the man who arrived in 1492, but to the peoples who were already here—and who are still here. It is past time our calendar said so.

Abolishing Columbus Day: Why the Nation Must Stop Celebrating a Legacy of Colonialism, Genocide, and Exploitation

Introduction

Each October, the United States pauses its routine to mark “Columbus Day”—a federal holiday that commemorates Christopher Columbus’s 1492 voyage to the Americas. Though framed as a celebration of discovery, the holiday enthrrones a figure whose arrival set in motion a cascade of violence, dispossession, and cultural annihilation for the Indigenous peoples who had thrived on the continent for millennia. In a nation that prizes truth, justice, and reconciliation, it is an affront to honor a man whose legacy is, at its core, one of colonial domination and systematic extermination.

The time has come for the United States to abolish Columbus Day as a federal holiday and replace it with a day that honestly reflects the country’s commitment to pluralism, historical accountability, and the rights of its first peoples. This essay argues that Columbus’s legacy is inseparably tied to colonialism, genocide, and exploitation; that the continued celebration of his “discovery” is an insult to the ancestors of the peoples he subjugated; and that abolishing the holiday is both a pragmatic and moral imperative for a nation striving toward genuine equity.

I. Columbus’s Voyage Initiated a Process of Colonial Conquest

  1. A “Discovery” Framed in Eurocentric Superiority
    Columbus’s 1492 expedition was sponsored by Spain to find a westward trade route to Asia. He never recognized that he had reached a continent already populated by millions of Indigenous peoples. His journals reveal a mindset of entitlement: “I was the first to discover these lands and to plant the flag of the sovereign King and Queen of Spain.” The notion of “discovery,” therefore, was a myth manufactured to legitimize European claims over lands that were not empty.

  2. The Legal Doctrine of Terra Discovery and Its Consequences
    The doctrine of terra nullius—the legal fiction that newly encountered lands were “empty” and could be claimed by the first European power—became a cornerstone of colonization. Columbus’s voyages gave birth to a legal precedent that justified the seizure of Indigenous territories, the imposition of European sovereignty, and the erasure of native governance structures. This framework paved the way for centuries of land grabs, treaty violations, and forced removals of Native peoples from their ancestral homelands.

  3. The Beginning of the Atlantic Slave Trade and Labor Exploitation
    Columbus’s arrival inaugurated a system of forced labor that would evolve into the transatlantic slave trade. Within months of landing on Hispaniola, he ordered the capture and shipment of Taíno individuals to Spain, describing them as “excellent and intelligent.” The encomienda system—granting colonists the right to extract labor from Indigenous peoples—enslaved thousands, leading to catastrophic mortality rates from overwork, disease, and malnutrition.

II. Columbus’s Governance Was a Blueprint for Genocide

  1. Systematic Violence and Massacre
    Columbus’s administration was marked by brutality. In his own words, he ordered the “cutting off of ears and noses” of natives who resisted, and he authorized the use of armed force to quell dissent. The 1495 Rebellion of the Taíno culminated in a retaliatory massacre that left hundreds dead and many more enslaved. Contemporary accounts describe the deliberate mutilation and slaughter of entire communities as punitive measures.

  2. Epidemic Catastrophe as an Indirect Weapon
    Columbus’s crew introduced Old World diseases—smallpox, measles, influenza—for which Indigenous peoples had no immunity. Within a generation, the native population of the Caribbean collapsed from an estimated 1–2 million to a few hundred thousand—a demographic decline exceeding 90 percent. While disease spread was unintentional, it was exacerbated by colonial policies that confined peoples to cramped settlements, forced labor, and malnutrition, accelerating mortality.

  3. Cultural Erasure and Religious Imposition
    Columbus and his successors imposed Spanish language, Catholic doctrine, and European customs on native peoples, dismantling longstanding spiritual and political systems. Missionary schools were used to eradicate Indigenous languages and histories, a process later termed “cultural genocide” by scholars of genocide studies. The deliberate suppression of native knowledge systems contributed to the loss of centuries of ecological wisdom, oral histories, and artistic traditions.

III. The Myth of Columbus as a National Hero Is a Misappropriation of History

  1. The “Heroic Narrative” Is a Construct Designed to Legitimize Expansionism
    In the early 20th century, Italian-American communities sought acceptance in a xenophobic United States. Columbus emerged as a convenient symbol, and the Knights of Columbus—a Catholic fraternal organization— championed a national holiday to honor him. This was less about celebrating a historical figure and more about cultivating a political narrative that validated the United States’ own expansionist destiny.

  2. Official Commemoration Obscures Ongoing Injustices
    By institutionalizing Columbus Day, the federal government implicitly condones the historical harms inflicted on Indigenous peoples. The holiday perpetuates a sanitized version of history that downplays or ignores the atrocities committed under Columbus’s command, thereby sustaining a collective amnesia about the genocide and exploitation that preceded modern America.

  3. The Holiday Contradicts Contemporary Values of Equity and Reconciliation
    The United States has formally recognized the United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples (UNDRIP) and has, in recent decades, passed legislation to protect Native American cultural heritage, language, and sovereignty. Continuing to celebrate Columbus Day—a commemoration of the very forces that undermined those rights—creates a glaring double standard that erodes trust in government commitments to justice.

IV. Alternatives Exist That Honor a More Honest National Narrative

  1. Indigenous Peoples’ Day as a Direct Replacement
    Over thirty U.S. states and several major cities already observe Indigenous Peoples’ Day—a day dedicated to honoring the histories, cultures, and contributions of Native peoples. This observance acknowledges the original stewards of the land and provides an opportunity for educational programming that centers Indigenous perspectives, rather than glorifying a colonizer.

  2. Educational Reform Can Replace Celebration with Critical Reflection
    Schools and public institutions can use the day to teach accurate historical content about the pre‑Columbian world, the impacts of European contact, and the ongoing struggles of Indigenous communities. By transforming the holiday into a platform for scholarship and dialogue, the nation can foster a deeper, more honest understanding of its origins.

  3. A Symbolic Shift Toward Reconciliation
    Abolishing Columbus Day would send an unequivocal message: the United States is willing to confront its painful past and to prioritize the dignity and rights of its first peoples. That symbolic shift can inspire legislative actions—such as honoring tribal sovereignty, fulfilling treaty obligations, and protecting sacred sites—by aligning national symbols with contemporary moral imperatives.

V. Counterarguments Rebutted

Counterargument Rebuttal
“Columbus Day honors Italian-American heritage, not genocide.” The celebration of heritage can be achieved through other, less contentious means—such as Italian-American cultural festivals, heritage months, or community scholarships. The holiday’s current national form conflates cultural pride with a glorified myth that marginalizes the victims of colonization.
“If we cancel Columbus Day, we erase history.” The purpose of public holidays is to commemorate events that positively shape national identity. History should not be celebrated merely because it happened; it must be evaluated against ethical standards. Erasing the specific symbol of Columbus preserves an incomplete story but allows for a more truthful and inclusive narrative to emerge.
“Other explorers committed atrocities; why single out Columbus?” Columbus is uniquely singled out because his voyages sparked the wave of European colonization that led to the systematic devastation of Indigenous societies across the Americas. He is the iconic figurehead of that transformation, and his holiday’s persistence institutionalizes a myth that obscures this pivotal historical juncture.
“It’s an innocuous tradition; it doesn’t cause real harm.” Public policy shapes cultural perception. When a nation officially honors a figure whose actions precipitated genocide, that endorsement normalizes historical denialism and perpetuates harm by reinforcing stereotypes and marginalization of Indigenous peoples. The cumulative effect of such endorsement is tangible in policymaking, public sentiment, and the lived experiences of Native communities.

Conclusion

Abolishing Columbus Day is not an attempt to erase history; it is an act of moral clarity—a necessary correction to a national narrative that has long celebrated a figure whose arrival unleashed centuries of suffering for Indigenous peoples. By removing a holiday that glorifies colonial conquest, the United States can:

  1. Acknowledge the full scope of its origins, including the violent displacement and genocide of Native nations.
  2. Replace a symbol of oppression with one of celebration and respect—Indigenous Peoples’ Day—thereby affirming the rights, cultures, and contributions of the continent’s original inhabitants.
  3. Align public policy with contemporary values of justice, equity, and reconciliation, strengthening the nation’s credibility at home and abroad.

The transition away from Columbus Day can be implemented through federal legislation, executive orders, and grassroots advocacy, ensuring a phased yet decisive shift. In its place, the United States has an unprecedented opportunity to forge a new collective memory—one that honors truth, respects sovereignty, and builds a future grounded on mutual respect rather than on the myth of a “discoverer” who brought devastation.

To abolish Columbus Day is to choose a path toward honest remembrance, genuine reconciliation, and a truly inclusive American identity.

Remove Columbus Day from the Federal Calendar: A Moral and Historical Imperative

Introduction

Every second Monday of October, the United States federal government closes its offices, pauses mail delivery, and observes a national holiday honoring Christopher Columbus — a man who never set foot on the North American continent, who died believing he had reached Asia, and whose expeditions initiated one of the most catastrophic sequences of violence, enslavement, and dispossession in recorded human history. Columbus Day is not merely an outdated tradition. It is an active endorsement, written into federal law, of the colonial project that decimated Indigenous populations across two continents. The United States should abolish Columbus Day as a federal holiday — not to erase history, but precisely because we must reckon honestly with it.

The argument for abolition rests on three converging pillars: the demonstrable historical record of Columbus's actions and their immediate consequences; the broader legacy of colonialism that his voyages inaugurated; and the profound moral contradiction of a pluralistic democracy celebrating a figure whose enterprise depended fundamentally on enslavement, genocide, and the denial of Indigenous humanity. These are not matters of interpretation or political sensitivity. They are documented facts that compel a serious reexamination of what the federal government chooses to honor.

Part I: The Historical Record Is Not in Dispute

Defenders of Columbus Day frequently appeal to mythology — Columbus as the brave visionary who "discovered" a new world and proved the earth was round, thereby launching the modern age of exploration and, eventually, American democracy. Nearly every component of this narrative is false, and the corrections are not recent revisionism. They are established historical scholarship.

Columbus did not prove the earth was round. Educated Europeans had accepted spherical earth theory since ancient Greece; Eratosthenes had calculated the earth's circumference with reasonable accuracy around 240 BCE. What Columbus actually miscalculated was the size of the earth — he dramatically underestimated it, which is why he believed he had reached Asia. He succeeded not because of superior knowledge, but because a continent he didn't know existed happened to be where he thought Asia was.

Columbus did not "discover" America. An estimated 50 to 100 million people already lived in the Western Hemisphere when he arrived in 1492 — sophisticated civilizations with complex governance, agriculture, astronomy, trade networks, and culture stretching back thousands of years. The Taíno people of the Caribbean, who first encountered Columbus on the island they called Guanahani, were not inhabitants of an empty wilderness awaiting European civilization. They were a developed society. The language of "discovery" is itself a remnant of the Doctrine of Discovery — a papal formulation used to justify European seizure of lands already occupied by non-Christian peoples, whose humanity was legally and theologically subordinated to European interests.

More importantly, Columbus did not merely arrive and observe. What he initiated in the years following 1492 — documented extensively in his own journals and letters, and in the accounts of contemporaries including Bartolomé de las Casas — constitutes a record of sustained brutality that would, by any modern legal standard, be classified as crimes against humanity.

In his own words, Columbus described the Taíno people as gentle, generous, and ripe for subjugation. His letters to the Spanish Crown proposed shipping Indigenous people to Spain as enslaved laborers, which he subsequently did. On his second voyage in 1495, Columbus organized the first mass slave raid in the Americas, capturing approximately 1,500 Taíno men, women, and children. He shipped 500 of them to Spain; roughly 200 died during the crossing. Those who remained on Hispaniola were subjected to a tribute system under which adult Taíno were required to deliver a quota of gold every three months. Those who failed — in a region that had limited gold deposits — had their hands cut off and were left to bleed to death. This is not accusation. Las Casas, who witnessed it, recorded it in detail. Columbus's own son Fernando acknowledged coercive labor practices in his biography of his father.

Under Columbus's governance of Hispaniola, the Taíno population collapsed with staggering speed. Estimates of the Taíno population on Hispaniola in 1492 range from several hundred thousand to over one million. By 1514 — just 22 years after Columbus's arrival — a Spanish census recorded approximately 22,000 Taíno remaining. By 1550, the population was functionally extinct on the island. The causes were inseparable: disease accelerated by the brutal conditions of forced labor, direct violence, systematic enslavement, and the destruction of the agricultural and social systems that had sustained Indigenous life for centuries. This is not background noise to Columbus's story. It is his story, particularly as governor of Hispaniola from 1493 to 1500, a position from which he was ultimately removed by Spanish authorities because his administration was considered excessively cruel even by the standards of 15th-century colonial governance.

The Spanish Crown eventually stripped Columbus of his titles and governorship following investigations into his rule. He was arrested and returned to Spain in chains in 1500. The historical Columbus — not the mythological one — was deemed too brutal to govern even a colony.

Part II: Columbus's Legacy Is Not Incidental — It Is the Point

Proponents of the holiday sometimes concede that Columbus was personally flawed while arguing that we celebrate him as a symbol of something larger: the spirit of exploration, Italian-American heritage, or the founding of Western civilization in the Americas. Each of these arguments, examined carefully, collapses.

The "symbol of exploration" argument treats Columbus as interchangeable with the abstract virtue of human curiosity and courage. But federal holidays do not honor abstractions — they honor specific individuals and specific events. We do not celebrate "military valor in general" on Veterans Day; we honor those who served in the United States Armed Forces. If we wished to honor the spirit of exploration, we could create a holiday honoring explorers whose expeditions did not begin with enslavement, or we could honor Indigenous peoples whose navigation, agriculture, and civilization constituted extraordinary human achievements predating European arrival by millennia. To insist on Columbus specifically as the vessel of this value requires ignoring what Columbus specifically did, which is not the celebration of exploration but its sanitization.

The Italian-American heritage argument deserves genuine respect as a cultural matter while being clearly separated from the federal holiday question. Columbus Day was formally established as a federal holiday in 1937, in significant part as a response to anti-Italian discrimination following the 1891 lynching of eleven Italian Americans in New Orleans, one of the largest mass lynchings in American history. The political logic was straightforward: elevate an Italian figure to national prominence to signal the legitimacy and Americanness of Italian immigrants and their descendants. This was a comprehensible response to real injustice.

However, the dignity and contributions of Italian Americans do not depend on, and should not be entangled with, the federal commemoration of Christopher Columbus specifically. Italian-American heritage is rich, complex, and celebrated across art, science, politics, labor, and culture. It does not require Columbus. Moreover, many Italian-American scholars, organizations, and community members have themselves advocated for Columbus Day's replacement, recognizing that community pride built on a foundation of documented atrocity is neither stable nor honorable. The question "should we honor Italian Americans?" has an easy answer: yes. The question "should we do so by honoring a man who pioneered transatlantic slavery?" has an equally clear answer: no. These are separable questions, and conflating them does a disservice to both Italian-American heritage and honest history.

The "founding of Western civilization" argument is perhaps the most revealing, because it most nakedly states what Columbus's holiday actually celebrates: the premise that European civilization's arrival in the Americas was an unqualified good — that whatever suffering accompanied it was either exaggerated, inevitable, or outweighed by the benefits of Christianity, democracy, and modernity that Europeans brought. This premise is both historically indefensible and morally corrosive. It requires one to weigh the lives of tens of millions of Indigenous people — their deaths, enslavement, cultural destruction, and ongoing dispossession — against abstract civilizational benefits, and to conclude the trade was acceptable. It requires treating Indigenous peoples as objects of history rather than its subjects, as problems to be overcome rather than people with inherent worth. A pluralistic democracy committed to human equality cannot coherently adopt this premise as a federal holiday.

Part III: The Ongoing Harm of Federal Commemoration

Columbus Day is not simply a relic with no present consequence. Federal holidays carry real weight — they communicate national values, they shape school curricula, they validate or invalidate certain historical narratives, and they send a message to living communities about whose suffering the country regards as worthy of acknowledgment.

For Indigenous peoples in the United States, Columbus Day functions as an annual federal declaration that the violence which initiated their dispossession is something their own government considers worth celebrating. The United States has a population of approximately 3.7 million people who identify as American Indian or Alaska Native alone. Their communities continue to suffer the documented, ongoing consequences of colonial policies: land dispossession, poverty rates dramatically higher than the national average, shortened life expectancy, epidemic rates of violence against Indigenous women, and the systematic destruction of languages and cultures that continues in many forms. These are not historical grievances. They are present realities, traceable in a direct and documented line from the colonial enterprise that Columbus inaugurated.

Against this backdrop, the federal government's annual celebration of Columbus is not neutral. It is a message. It says that the origins of this suffering — the initial act of treating Indigenous peoples as bodies to be exploited and lands to be seized — belongs in the category of things the United States honors rather than the category of things it regrets. This is not a message consistent with a government that claims to be committed to equal dignity under law.

Thirty-six states have already changed the observance in some form. More than 130 cities and several states now officially celebrate Indigenous Peoples' Day in place of or alongside Columbus Day. This is not a radical fringe movement. It is a growing democratic consensus reflecting honest historical reckoning. Cities including Los Angeles, Denver, Phoenix, and Seattle — and states including California, Oregon, Minnesota, and New Mexico — have concluded that the federal holiday does not reflect their values or accurately represent history. The federal government is increasingly isolated in its official position, maintaining a commemoration that an expanding majority of Americans, including significant portions of the Italian-American community, do not believe serves any legitimate purpose.

Part IV: Responding to Common Objections

"We can't judge historical figures by modern standards."

This objection sounds reasonable in the abstract but fails scrutiny in application. Columbus was not operating in a moral vacuum in which the harm of slavery was unknown. He was confronted by Taíno people who were, by his own written account, peaceful, generous, and fully human in their behavior toward him. Las Casas and other contemporaries explicitly condemned the treatment of Indigenous peoples in Columbus's time using moral language available to them. The Catholic Church itself engaged extensive theological debate about the humanity and rights of Indigenous peoples in the 16th century. The condemnation of Columbus's conduct is not anachronistic — it was voiced in his own era. Moreover, even if we bracket the moral question entirely, the objection cuts in both directions: if we cannot judge historical figures by modern standards, we equally cannot celebrate them by modern standards. You cannot invoke "different times" to shield Columbus from criticism while simultaneously placing him on a pedestal meant to represent values — courage, ingenuity, multicultural heritage — articulated through a modern moral lens.

"Removing the holiday erases history."

Abolishing a celebration is not the same as erasing memory. Germany does not celebrate Hitler's birthday, and this does not mean the Holocaust is forgotten — in fact, Germany has been far more honest about confronting that history than the United States has been about confronting Indigenous genocide, in part because no federal holiday frames the perpetrators as heroes requiring commemoration. School curricula, museums, books, and scholarship preserve and examine Columbus's voyages in detail and should continue to do so. A federal holiday is not a history lesson — it is an endorsement. Removing the endorsement does not remove the history; it restores something closer to historical honesty.

"This is just political correctness."

Describing accurate history as "political correctness" is a rhetorical move that substitutes dismissal for argument. The documented facts of Columbus's governance — the slavery, the mutilation, the population collapse — are not contested among historians in any serious way. They are in primary sources. Calling the moral implications of those facts "political correctness" suggests that accuracy and human empathy are somehow illegitimate standards for evaluating a federal holiday. That is not a defensible position.

Part V: What Should Replace It

The question of replacement is practically important and morally illuminating. Many advocates, including the Indigenous Peoples' Day movement, propose that the second Monday of October become a federal holiday honoring Indigenous peoples — their civilizations, their survival, their ongoing contributions to American life, and their historical experience of colonization. This is not a punitive proposal. It does not demand that anyone feel guilty or perform atonement. It asks that the federal government acknowledge, with the weight a federal holiday carries, that the peoples who inhabited this land for thousands of years before European arrival deserve recognition and honor.

Such a holiday would serve multiple legitimate purposes simultaneously. It would provide an honest corrective to a historical narrative that has long subordinated Indigenous perspectives. It would honor the genuine heritage and contributions of Native Americans in a meaningful, federally recognized way. It would demonstrate to Indigenous communities that their government is capable of honest reckoning with the colonial origins it has long minimized. And it would model for American schoolchildren a form of patriotism that is compatible with truth — the understanding that a nation can acknowledge the worst of its origins while committing to better values going forward.

This is also not unprecedented in American history. The United States has revised its national commemorations before. Columbus Day itself was not a federal holiday until 1937. Martin Luther King Jr. Day was established in 1983 over significant political resistance and is now widely celebrated. The arc of national commemoration can bend toward greater honesty, and it has before.

Conclusion

The case for abolishing Columbus Day is not a case against history — it is a case for facing it. Christopher Columbus initiated a process that killed tens of millions of people, enslaved Indigenous populations across the Caribbean, and established the template of colonial violence and dispossession that shaped the Western Hemisphere for the following five centuries. He did so with documented intentionality, was removed from his own position for excessive cruelty, and died having initiated consequences of incalculable human suffering. The United States federal government currently sets aside a day every year to honor this man.

The foundation of a just democratic society is the premise that all people possess equal dignity and that the suffering of any human community matters. We cannot coherently hold this premise while simultaneously maintaining a federal holiday whose entire significance depends on treating the Indigenous peoples Columbus enslaved and destroyed as background figures in a story of European heroism. The moral logic is simple, even if the politics are contested: a nation that claims to value human dignity should not celebrate those who trampled it on a mass scale.

Abolish Columbus Day. Replace it with a federal holiday honoring Indigenous peoples. Do not do it because history is easy or comfortable, but because honest democracies must be capable of that kind of serious reckoning. The second Monday of October can become not a day of historical denial, but a day of historical acknowledgment — and in that transformation, something genuinely worth celebrating would emerge.
