A Case for Abolishing Columbus Day: Reckoning with History and Honoring Humanity

Introduction

Every October, federal offices close, mail stops, and banks shut their doors in observance of a holiday that honors Christopher Columbus — the Genoese navigator whose 1492 voyage inaugurated an era of European colonization in the Americas. Columbus Day has been a federal holiday since 1937, embedded in the civic calendar of the United States as though it were an uncontested celebration of discovery and progress. But in the decades since its establishment, a growing chorus of historians, Indigenous communities, educators, and lawmakers has raised a fundamental objection: Christopher Columbus is not a figure who deserves federal celebration. His legacy is not one of heroic exploration but of colonial violence, enslavement, and the catastrophic destruction of Indigenous civilizations.

The argument for abolishing Columbus Day is not an argument for erasing history. It is an argument for telling history honestly, and for using the civic calendar — a reflection of national values — to honor people and principles worthy of the republic's stated ideals. The case is built on three pillars: the historical record of Columbus's actions, the moral incoherence of celebrating colonial conquest in a pluralistic democracy, and the existence of better alternatives that serve both historical accuracy and national unity.

I. The Historical Record: Columbus as Perpetrator, Not Hero

The popular mythology of Columbus — the brave visionary who sailed into the unknown to prove the earth was round — is a nineteenth-century fabrication layered over a far darker reality. The historical Columbus, documented extensively in his own letters and journals, as well as in the accounts of contemporaries like Bartolomé de las Casas, was an agent of exploitation whose voyages set in motion one of the most devastating processes of conquest and depopulation in human history.

Enslavement from the First Voyage

Upon landing in the Bahamas in October 1492, Columbus encountered the Taíno people, whom he described in his journal as gentle, generous, and physically admirable. His response to this generosity was not reciprocity but calculation. He wrote to the Spanish Crown that the Taíno "would make fine servants" and that "with fifty men we could subjugate them all and make them do whatever we want." Even on this first voyage, Columbus kidnapped several dozen Taíno individuals and brought them to Spain, where many died during the crossing. Seven surviving captives were presented at the Spanish court — not as honored guests, but as curiosities and proof of a new labor source.

The Governorship and Systematic Brutality

When Columbus returned on his second voyage, he came not merely as an explorer but as governor of the newly claimed territories. His administration of Hispaniola constituted a regime of terror. He imposed a tribute system requiring every Taíno person over the age of fourteen to deliver a regular quota of gold dust. Those who failed to meet the quota had their hands cut off. Columbus and his men enslaved thousands of Indigenous people, sending them in chains to Spain, where they were sold at auction. Estimates suggest that by 1495, Columbus had enslaved approximately 1,500 Taíno people, with around 500 shipped to Europe.

Bartolomé de las Casas, a Spanish priest who later became a fierce advocate for Indigenous rights, arrived in Hispaniola in 1502 and documented the devastation. He described mass killings, torture, and a regime so brutal that it shocked even Spanish contemporaries. Las Casas's A Short Account of the Destruction of the Indies (1552) remains one of the most harrowing primary sources of the era. While some historians caution that Las Casas's figures may be inflated, the broad pattern of violence and exploitation is corroborated by Columbus's own letters and by the archaeological record.

Catastrophic Depopulation

The demographic consequences were staggering. Pre-contact population estimates for Hispaniola vary — some scholars place the Taíno population between 250,000 and over one million. By the mid-sixteenth century, within sixty years of Columbus's arrival, the Indigenous population of the island had been effectively annihilated. The causes were multiple — epidemic disease, forced labor, mass killings, famine, and the social collapse that accompanied conquest — but Columbus's policies of enslavement and forced tribute were primary engines of this catastrophe.

It is true that European diseases, particularly smallpox, were the single largest killer of Indigenous peoples throughout the Americas, and Columbus himself did not introduce disease deliberately. But this fact does not absolve his regime. Disease was compounded by the conditions of enslavement, malnutrition, and displacement that Columbus's administration imposed. The Taíno did not merely die of illness; they were worked to death in mines and plantations by a system Columbus designed and enforced.

Posthumous Conviction

The historical record does not rely solely on critics. Columbus's contemporaries in Spain itself recognized the severity of his abuses. In 1500, the Spanish Crown sent Francisco de Bobadilla to Hispaniola to investigate reports of tyranny. Bobadilla arrested Columbus and his brothers, shackled them, and shipped them back to Spain in chains. Columbus spent weeks in prison. While he was eventually released, he was permanently stripped of his governorship. The Spanish Crown — hardly a paragon of Indigenous rights — found Columbus's conduct so egregious that it removed him from power.

II. The Moral Incoherence of Federal Celebration

A federal holiday is not a neutral administrative designation. It is a statement of collective values, an instruction to citizens about what their nation considers worthy of honor. When the United States declares a day of observance for a historical figure, it performs an act of civic endorsement. The question, then, is not whether Columbus existed or whether his voyages were historically significant — they unquestionably were — but whether the federal government should formally celebrate him.

The Distinction Between Commemoration and Celebration

Nobody is proposing that Christopher Columbus be stricken from history textbooks. His voyages remain a turning point in world history, and any serious education about the Americas must grapple with the consequences of 1492. But there is a fundamental difference between studying a historical figure and celebrating one. We study Genghis Khan, the Black Death, and the institution of slavery without declaring holidays in their honor. The federal calendar should distinguish between acknowledging significance and bestowing honor. Columbus's voyages are historically significant. Columbus himself, given the totality of his actions, is not a figure who merits the honor of a federal holiday.

The Signal to Indigenous Communities

For Indigenous peoples in the United States, Columbus Day is not merely an outdated tradition — it is an annual reminder of a history of erasure and dehumanization. The federal government, by celebrating Columbus, implicitly endorses the narrative that the "discovery" of the Americas was an unambiguous good, that the lands were empty or that their inhabitants were obstacles to progress. This narrative directly contradicts the lived experience and historical memory of Indigenous communities who experienced colonization as catastrophe.

A government that has acknowledged — through official apologies, through the establishment of the National Museum of the American Indian, through decades of policy reform — the injustices inflicted upon Indigenous peoples cannot coherently maintain a holiday that celebrates the individual who inaugurated those injustices. The abolition of Columbus Day is not an act of political correctness; it is an act of moral consistency.

The Problem of Whitewashing

The continued celebration of Columbus Day perpetuates a sanitized version of history that serves no one well. When children are taught that Columbus was a brave explorer who "discovered" America, they are being taught a narrative that omits slavery, mass death, and colonial domination. When they later encounter the historical record — in college, in independent reading, in conversations with Indigenous peers — the dissonance breeds cynicism and distrust. A nation that is confident in its values should be confident enough to tell its history honestly. Abolishing Columbus Day and replacing it with a more accurate observance would strengthen, not weaken, civic education.

III. The Practical and Political Precedent

The movement to abolish Columbus Day is not speculative. It is already well underway, and the results offer a model for federal action.

State and Local Action

As of the mid-2020s, more than a dozen states and over 130 cities have replaced Columbus Day with Indigenous Peoples' Day or have adopted the latter alongside it. States including Vermont, Maine, New Mexico, and Alaska have made the change through legislation or executive order. Cities as diverse as Los Angeles, Denver, Seattle, Phoenix, and Minneapolis have done the same. These are not marginal jurisdictions; they represent millions of Americans who already observe an alternative to Columbus Day.

Institutional Shifts

Universities, school districts, and cultural institutions have increasingly moved away from Columbus Day observance. The movement reflects a broader scholarly consensus that the traditional Columbus narrative is historically inadequate and ethically troubling. When the institutions responsible for education and historical memory have already shifted, the federal government's continued insistence on Columbus Day looks less like principled tradition and more like institutional inertia.

The Federal Response

In 2021, President Joe Biden became the first sitting president to issue a proclamation recognizing Indigenous Peoples' Day alongside Columbus Day. While this was a symbolic step, it stopped short of the structural change that advocates seek. The federal holiday remains Columbus Day. Executive proclamations can be reversed by subsequent administrations; only congressional action to replace Columbus Day with a new federal holiday would establish a durable change.

The Alternative: Indigenous Peoples' Day

The most commonly proposed replacement is Indigenous Peoples' Day — a day dedicated to honoring the histories, cultures, and contributions of Indigenous peoples, both those who lived before European contact and those who continue to thrive today. This alternative achieves several things simultaneously: it corrects the historical record, it centers the experiences of communities that have been marginalized for centuries, and it provides an occasion for the kind of civic reflection and education that a holiday is meant to encourage.

Indigenous Peoples' Day does not erase history; it reframes it. It does not deny that Columbus's voyages were consequential; it insists that the consequences be understood honestly. And it does not exclude any community from the civic fold; it invites all Americans to engage with the full complexity of their shared past.

IV. Addressing Counterarguments

"Columbus was a man of his time."

This defense proves too much. Many historical figures operated within the moral frameworks of their eras. But a federal holiday is not an exercise in contextual empathy — it is an act of contemporary civic endorsement. We do not celebrate every figure who behaved according to the norms of their era; we select those whose actions and values we wish to elevate. Columbus's contemporaries, including Spanish officials and clergy, recognized the extremity of his cruelty. The "man of his time" argument, moreover, could be used to excuse virtually any historical atrocity, which is precisely why it is insufficient as a basis for national celebration.

"Columbus Day honors Italian-American heritage."

This is the strongest argument in favor of retaining the holiday, and it deserves a respectful response. Italian-Americans faced genuine discrimination in the United States, particularly in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries. The establishment of Columbus Day in 1937 was, in part, a recognition of Italian-American contributions and a response to anti-Italian prejudice. This history matters, and Italian-American heritage deserves celebration.

But it does not follow that Christopher Columbus must be the vehicle for that celebration. Italy and the Italian diaspora have produced an extraordinary wealth of figures worthy of honor — scientists, artists, political leaders, and community builders whose legacies are unburdened by genocide and enslavement. A holiday dedicated to Italian-American heritage, attached to a figure of unambiguous merit, would serve the community far better than a holiday that forces Italian-Americans to defend a deeply compromised historical figure every October. Many Italian-Americans themselves have made this argument, and organizations representing Indigenous and Italian-American communities have found common ground on the question.

"This is erasing history."

Abolishing a federal holiday does not erase history. The abolition of a holiday is not the burning of archives or the banning of books. History is preserved in scholarship, in museums, in textbooks, and in public memory — not in the federal holiday calendar. The United States has abolished holidays before without erasing the events they commemorated. The argument confuses civic celebration with historical record, and it assumes that the only way to remember the past is to formally honor it — a premise that no serious historian would endorse.

V. A Call for Moral Clarity

The case for abolishing Columbus Day ultimately rests on a simple proposition: a democratic republic should use its civic calendar to honor figures and principles that reflect its highest aspirations. Christopher Columbus does not meet that standard. His voyages opened the door to centuries of colonization, dispossession, and genocide. His personal conduct — documented by his own hand and by his contemporaries — included enslavement, torture, and the brutal exploitation of Indigenous peoples. To celebrate him with a federal holiday is to endorse, however passively, the values that animated his colonial project.

Abolishing Columbus Day would not be an act of political division. It would be an act of historical honesty and moral seriousness. It would signal that the United States is capable of reckoning with the full scope of its history — the beauty and the brutality — and that it is willing to use its civic institutions not to sanitize the past, but to learn from it.

The replacement of Columbus Day with Indigenous Peoples' Day — or with any observance that accurately reflects the complexity of 1492 and its aftermath — would be a step toward a more truthful, more inclusive, and more morally coherent national identity. It would tell Indigenous communities that their history matters. It would tell students that their government trusts them with the truth. And it would tell the world that the United States is a nation confident enough in its ideals to examine them honestly.

The time has come to close the book on Columbus Day and open a new one.

This essay presents one perspective in an ongoing civic debate. Readers are encouraged to consult primary sources, engage with multiple viewpoints, and form their own informed conclusions.

For over a century, the United States has celebrated Christopher Columbus as a heroic explorer through an official federal holiday. Schoolchildren learn a sanitized narrative: in 1492, Columbus "sailed the ocean blue" and "discovered" America, courageously bridging continents. This myth erases both the existence of sophisticated Indigenous civilizations and Columbus's own brutal record. Columbus's journals reveal his immediate impulse toward domination upon encountering the Taíno people of the Caribbean. Writing to Spanish patrons, he described Indigenous people as ideal slaves: "They would make fine servants... With fifty men we could subjugate them all and make them do whatever we want."

By 1495, Columbus had initiated a systemic campaign of terror. He enslaved thousands of Taíno people, shipping over 1,500 to Spain in chains – many perishing en route – and implemented the encomienda system, forcing survivors into labor camps to mine gold under torturous conditions. Those who failed to meet quotas had hands severed. Famine, disease, and mass executions followed. Bartolomé de las Casas, a Spanish colonist turned priest who witnessed these atrocities, documented infants being dashed against rocks and "testing" swords on naked villagers. Within decades, the Taíno population plummeted from an estimated 250,000–300,000 to near extinction.

Columbus was no rogue agent. His governance as Viceroy of the Indies was so vicious that Spanish authorities arrested him for excessive brutality. His legacy ignited centuries of colonial violence across the Americas. Celebrating him validates this genocide as a historical inevitability rather than a crime against humanity.

Maintaining Columbus Day perpetuates three profound harms:

  1. Trauma and Erasure: For Indigenous communities, the holiday is a grotesque celebration of their ancestors' exterminators. It imposes a state-sanctioned narrative that marginalizes Native survivance – a term emphasizing active resistance and continuity – and sanitizes a cultural cataclysm.   2. Educational Malpractice: By uncritically honoring Columbus, schools propagate settler-colonial myths that distort young people's understanding of history. This feeds racist stereotypes, undermining contemporary struggles for Indigenous sovereignty and environmental justice.

  3. Moral Hypocrisy: The United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples condemns celebrating colonial figures. America's continued adherence to Columbus Day contradicts its professed commitments to human rights.

Replacing Columbus Day with Indigenous Peoples' Day corrects historical injustice while celebrating vibrant Native cultures. Since Berkeley, California, pioneered this change in 1992, over 17 states and 190 cities have followed suit – often led by Native activists. This holiday acknowledges:

Title: Unmaking the Myth: The Moral Imperative to Abolish Columbus Day

For over a century, the United States has paused every October to honor Christopher Columbus, a figure mythologized in American classrooms as the intrepid explorer who "discovered" the New World. This narrative, enshrined in a federal holiday, frames the events of 1492 as the heroic genesis of the Americas. However, historical record and primary sources reveal a starkly different reality: one of colonization, systematic exploitation, and genocide. Federal holidays are not merely days off; they are statements of national identity and values. By maintaining Columbus Day, the United States government implicitly endorses a legacy of brutality and erasure. To align national symbols with historical truth and modern human rights standards, the United States must abolish Columbus Day and redirect that recognition toward the Indigenous peoples who survived the onslaught he initiated.

The argument for abolishing Columbus Day begins with the dismantling of the historical myth. Columbus was not a benign navigator who accidentally stumbled upon inhabited lands; he was an ambitious venture capitalist of his era, motivated primarily by the acquisition of gold and the subjugation of human beings. Upon his arrival in the Bahamas, Columbus noted in his own codified journals the hospitality of the Arawak and Taino peoples, yet immediately viewed them through the lens of exploitation. He wrote, "They would make fine servants... With fifty men we could subjugate them all and make them do whatever we want." This clearly demonstrates that his intent was never mutual exchange or diplomacy, but domination and commodification.

The specifics of Columbus’s governance in Hispaniola (modern-day Haiti and the Dominican Republic) provide the most damning evidence against his celebration. Under his administration, Columbus instituted a tribute system that required Indigenous persons over the age of fourteen to supply a quota of gold or spun cotton. Those who failed to meet these quotas had their hands cut off and were left to bleed to death. This reign of terror was not a product of inevitable "cultural misunderstanding" or passive disease transmission; it was active, administrative cruelty. Contemporary observers, including the Spanish priest Bartolomé de las Casas, documented these atrocities, describing how Spanish occupiers committed massacres, tested the sharpness of their blades on living bodies, and engaged in mass suicides to escape the brutality. To celebrate Columbus is to celebrate the architect of this nightmare.

Furthermore, Columbus serves as the progenitor of the transatlantic slave trade, a system that would haunt the Americas for centuries. Failing to find the immense gold reserves he had promised the Spanish monarchs, Columbus turned to the only other resource he recognized: human bodies. He sent thousands of Taino people across the ocean to likely death in Spain and instituted the encomienda system, a form of feudal slavery, in the Caribbean. Moreover, his letters reveal a disturbing complicity in sex trafficking, noting that girls as young as nine were in high demand by his men. It is morally incoherent for a nation that fought a civil war to end slavery and claims to champion human rights to maintain a federal holiday honoring a man who commodified human life on an industrial scale.

Defenders of the holiday often argue that Columbus Day is a necessary celebration of Italian-American heritage, established as a response to anti-Italian discrimination in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. While the contribution of Italian-Americans to the fabric of the United States is undeniable and worthy of celebration, hinging that pride on Christopher Columbus is a fatal error. Heritage cannot be used as a shield to protect the reputation of a tyrant. There are countless Italian figures—artists, thinkers, scientists, and humanitarians—who represent the best of that culture without the baggage of genocide. Continuing to use Columbus as a mascot for Italian-American pride forces a false choice between honoring an immigrant community and respecting the humanity of Indigenous peoples.

Finally, the continuation of Columbus Day perpetuates the erasure of Indigenous history. For Native Americans, Columbus is not a symbol of discovery, but the face of an apocalypse—the beginning of centuries of displacement, broken treaties, and cultural destruction. A federal holiday honoring him sends a clear message from the government to its Indigenous citizens: your suffering is irrelevant, and your oppressor is a hero. Abolishing Columbus Day and replacing it with Indigenous Peoples’ Day is an essential step toward transitional justice. It shifts the focus from the colonizer to the survival, resilience, and rich cultural contributions of the First Nations.

A society defines itself by whom it chooses to honor. Monuments and holidays are not neutral; they are the pillars of our collective memory. By clinging to Columbus Day, the United States clings to a colonial fantasy that values conquest over humanity. The historical evidence of Columbus’s crimes—torture, slavery, and mass killing—is overwhelming and undisputed by serious scholarship. We cannot change history, but we can change how we regard it. Abolishing Columbus Day is not an act of erasing history; it is an act of correcting it, prioritizing truth over tradition, and affirming that the United States values justice over the glorification of exploitation.

It promotes the idea that American heritage is not solely defined by European roots but is deeply indebted to the original inhabitants of the land.

Conclusion

The shift from Columbus Day to Indigenous Peoples' Day is viewed by its supporters as an act of restorative justice. By ceasing to glorify a figure associated with genocide and instead honoring the victims and survivors of colonization, society signals a commitment to truth-telling and inclusivity. The goal is to transform a national holiday from a source of pain for Native communities into a celebration of their enduring spirit and contributions.

Model Response:

Columbus Day should be abolished as a federal holiday because it asks the United States to officially honor a man whose historical legacy is inseparable from colonial violence, Indigenous dispossession, slavery, and atrocity. Federal holidays are not neutral dates on a calendar; they are national endorsements. They signal who and what the country chooses to commemorate. To continue celebrating Christopher Columbus in that way is to ignore the devastating human consequences of his voyages and the system of conquest they helped unleash. If a federal holiday is meant to reflect national values, then Columbus Day fails that test. A nation that claims to value human dignity, equality, and historical truth should not dedicate a day of honor to a figure so closely associated with the destruction of Native societies.

The traditional defense of Columbus Day rests on an outdated heroic narrative: that Columbus was a bold explorer who “discovered” America and opened a new chapter in world history. But this narrative collapses under even basic historical scrutiny. Columbus did not “discover” an empty land. The Americas were already populated by millions of Indigenous people with sophisticated civilizations, political systems, trade networks, spiritual traditions, and deep relationships to their lands. To describe Columbus as a discoverer is to erase those peoples and treat their existence as irrelevant. It reflects a colonial worldview in which land only becomes real when Europeans arrive to claim it. That language is not harmless. It encodes the same mindset that justified conquest, seizure, and domination.

More importantly, Columbus was not simply a man of his time caught in a harsh era. His own record reveals deliberate brutality. On Hispaniola, under Columbus’s rule, Indigenous Taíno people were subjected to forced labor, tribute demands, mutilation, kidnapping, and mass killing. Those who could not meet impossible quotas of gold faced savage punishment. Women and girls were exploited sexually. Indigenous communities were torn apart, their social order shattered by enslavement, violence, disease, and starvation. While Columbus was not the sole architect of all the horrors that followed European invasion, he was a direct participant in, and catalyst for, a regime of exploitation. Honoring him sanitizes these crimes and transforms suffering into pageantry.

Some defenders argue that Columbus should still be commemorated because his voyages changed world history. But historical significance is not the same as moral worthiness. Many figures altered the course of history through conquest, cruelty, or oppression; that does not mean they deserve celebration. A federal holiday is not a history lesson. It is an act of praise. No one denies that Columbus mattered. The question is whether he merits honor. A person can be historically pivotal and still be wholly unfit for public veneration. In fact, the very magnitude of Columbus’s impact makes celebration more offensive, because the chain of events linked to his voyages includes centuries of Indigenous land theft, forced conversion, cultural destruction, slavery, and genocide.

The word genocide is not rhetorical excess in this context. While historians may debate specific legal categories or causal mechanisms in every instance, there is no serious doubt that Indigenous populations across the Americas suffered catastrophic destruction as a result of European colonization, and Columbus’s expeditions were among its earliest turning points. His governance helped inaugurate systems that treated Native people as exploitable bodies rather than human beings. Even where disease played a major role in demographic collapse, violence, forced labor, famine, displacement, and terror intensified the devastation. The moral problem is not reduced by saying that many died from illness rather than the sword. Colonialism was not merely accidental contact; it was a structure of domination that exploited vulnerability and compounded death. Columbus stands at the symbolic beginning of that structure.

Continuing to celebrate Columbus Day also causes real harm in the present. Public memory matters. The stories nations elevate shape how citizens understand justice, belonging, and whose pain counts. For Indigenous peoples, Columbus Day is not an abstract historical dispute. It is a yearly reminder that the federal government still honors a symbol of invasion and devastation while Indigenous communities continue to face the consequences of colonization: poverty, land loss, underfunded schools, broken treaties, environmental injustice, and the suppression of languages and traditions. To insist on preserving Columbus Day is to prioritize a comforting myth for some Americans over the historical trauma and lived reality of others. That is not national unity; it is moral evasion.

Abolishing Columbus Day would not mean erasing history. On the contrary, it would represent a commitment to teaching history more honestly. Critics often frame the removal of honors from controversial figures as an attack on the past, but there is a profound difference between remembering and revering. Schools, museums, books, and public discussion should absolutely continue to examine Columbus and the age of European exploration. But examination is not celebration. A mature society does not need to convert every historically important figure into a hero. It should be capable of confronting uncomfortable truths and revising its commemorations accordingly. If anything, abolishing the holiday would encourage a more accurate and responsible public understanding of history.

Another argument sometimes made in defense of Columbus Day is that the holiday has become an important symbol of Italian American pride and recognition, especially given the discrimination Italian immigrants once faced in the United States. That history of anti-Italian prejudice is real and deserves acknowledgment. But Christopher Columbus is a poor vessel for that recognition. Ethnic pride should not depend on elevating a man associated with enslavement and colonial terror. Italian American heritage is rich with artists, labor leaders, scientists, public servants, activists, and cultural figures who can be honored without asking Indigenous people to celebrate their own historical dispossession. Preserving Columbus Day in the name of Italian American identity wrongly assumes that one community’s dignity requires another community’s pain. It does not.

Replacing Columbus Day with Indigenous Peoples’ Day is a far better alternative. Such a change would not merely remove an offensive symbol; it would affirm the presence, resilience, and sovereignty of the first peoples of these lands. Indigenous Peoples’ Day invites Americans to learn about Native histories that long predate European arrival and that continue into the present. It shifts the focus from conquest to survival, from imperial myth to human complexity, from glorifying domination to recognizing endurance and cultural richness. That is a far more worthy basis for national reflection. A federal holiday should encourage values the country aspires to embody. Respect for Indigenous peoples, truth-telling about history, and rejection of colonial violence are values worth honoring.

Some will say abolishing Columbus Day judges the past by present moral standards. But this objection is overstated and often selectively applied. Even in Columbus’s own time, there were critics of Spanish brutality toward Indigenous peoples. The claim that “everyone thought this way” is historically false and ethically evasive. More fundamentally, the issue is not whether people in the fifteenth century met twenty-first century ideals. The issue is whether the United States today should place its stamp of approval on Columbus through a federal holiday. We are not obligated to preserve old honors simply because they were established in a less morally informed era. Public commemoration is always a choice, and choices can be revised when they no longer reflect deeper understanding or better values.

Abolishing Columbus Day would be a modest but meaningful act of moral clarity. It would acknowledge that the nation can no longer separate Columbus from the violence his name represents. It would tell Indigenous peoples that their history matters more than a sanitized national legend. It would show that Americans are capable of confronting the darker foundations of their history rather than hiding behind euphemism and nostalgia. It would also help dismantle a triumphalist narrative in which European arrival is treated as the unquestioned beginning of significance in the Americas. That narrative has long justified exclusion and inequality. Rejecting it is part of building a more truthful and just national memory.

In the end, the question is simple: whom should a nation honor? A federal holiday should be reserved for people or principles that elevate the country’s ideals, not for a figure whose legacy is bound to conquest, cruelty, and the dehumanization of Indigenous peoples. Christopher Columbus was not merely an explorer. He was a central symbol of a colonial enterprise that brought immeasurable suffering. To continue celebrating him is to perpetuate historical falsehood and moral blindness. The United States should abolish Columbus Day as a federal holiday and replace it with a commemoration that reflects truth, justice, and respect for the first peoples of this continent.
